idiom_name: programmed expectations on a substituted collaborator (hand-written or generated)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: construct a test-specific object that implements the collaborator's interface, programme the calls the system under test must make - method, argument matchers, cardinality, order, and the return value or exception for each - then install it through the substitutable dependency the SUT supports (constructor/setter injection or lookup) before exercising the SUT. During exercise the double compares every received call against the programmed expectations and fails the test at the first deviation; after exercise a final verification step reports expectations that were never fulfilled. Keep the expectation list at exactly the strength the requirement implies, verify the SUT's own results separately, and keep at least one double-free test to prove the real collaborator honours the assumed contract.
code_sketch:
mock = mock_of(Warehouse)
mock.expect("hasInventory", "Talisker", 50).returns(true)  # configure BEFORE
mock.expect("remove", "Talisker", 50).times(1)
install(order, mock)          # substitutable dependency
order.fill()                  # exercise: the mock checks each call as it arrives
verify(mock)                  # final verification: no expectation left unmet
pitfalls: Configuring expectations after the mock has been handed to the code under test is undefined in most frameworks and silently disables checking.
A double for a collaborator you do not own encodes your assumption about a contract nobody verifies; one double-free test per contract is the counterweight.
Expectations stricter than the requirement (exact order, exact counts) turn behaviour-preserving refactorings into failures and push teams to loosen or delete the checks.

Wrong move: use Python's permissive Mock for a collaborator whose signature is part of the contract -> renamed or missing arguments can pass in tests and fail only in production -> instead use create_autospec or autospec and pair it with a real-implementation contract test.

Wrong move: apply Mockito verifyNoMoreInteractions in every test -> harmless implementation changes become brittle failures -> instead verify only interactions required by the behaviour, reserving no-more checks for explicit no-extra-call requirements.
